utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Alex Demirdjian for the Prosecution, joined by Thomas Laugel, our Case Manager, and our intern, Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be brought in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, General. May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to return to the issue of Town Commands, which I was asking you questions about when we concluded your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'd like to bring up on the screen 65 ter 6106. This is tab 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a 1st Mechanised Corps report to the 1st Military District, dated 25 February 1992. And if we turn to the last page. And if we turn to the last page, we'll be able to see that it's submitted by Major-General Mico Delic. And I'd like to draw your attention to page 2 of this report where Major-General Delic reports on a number of objective difficulties faced by the civilian affairs organs, including, and I believe this is the second bullet point, or about midway through the page, he raises the difficulty of the selection of civilian authority organs is the responsibility of the Executive Councils of the government of SAO SBWS; most often -- and municipalities: "Most often these are their people. If we directly involve ourselves in the selection of these people, it would cause dissatisfaction on the part of the government and its institutions, and even the people." General, were the JNA Town Commands permitted to involve themselves in local politics?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they would just make their observations and assessments. This is simply a statement as to what the situation was and that there are difficulties regarding elections of civilian authorities on the ground, so this is just within the context of this being advisory organs rendering some kind of assistance in establishing a system of government and for having all spheres of life start functioning on the ground. If certain checks were made though and if they had some information about certain persons who would not exactly be eligible to hold a particular post, they could have passed that on, but it wasn't in their hands to decide who it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who would they pass that information on to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically regarding the situation and problems with establishing civilian government, it's send to the -- from the corps to the 1st Military District, and in the 1st Military District there was a special organ that was in charge of these problems regarding Town Commands and then that report would be sent to them. If there would be some problems in their functioning, they were actually not in charge of resolving disputes and passing judgement. Their reports were sent to the Command of the Military District and then, according to those instructions, they were supposed to inform the government of Serbia about that, and then the government of Serbia would exercise influence vis-a-vis the organs of government in the territory of the SBWS. That's why some of these problems are being indicated here, described.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why was the selection of civilian authority organs causing problems in the SBWS in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw some of these reports from different levels, from brigade level to the level of corps. The problem boils down to the following: On the one hand, in certain areas, the population itself opposed the functioning of these authorities. In such reports, it was indicated that there were still quite a few Croats in particular areas, and they distanced themselves from these activities. They didn't want to take part. Also, there was resistance on the part of others because they disagreed with certain candidates who were supposed to hold a particular position in their territory. So then there was this tacit obstruction, if you will. I saw such reports coming from lower levels. Also, there were objections to the effect that there were different personal connections involved, in terms of who would hold which particular office. This was not characteristic only of the situation in the SBWS, but it's characteristic of areas beyond that in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify your last answer, General, you just testified that in such reports it was indicated: "... that there were still quite a few Croats in particular areas, and they distanced themselves from these activities." Who was distancing themselves from these activities, and what were these activities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in one report - I don't know whether it was from the 2nd Brigade of the corps - they indicated that Croats did not want to take part in the these activities regarding the appointment of particular organs, their functioning, et cetera, and, generally speaking, that they are resisting the whole effort. This was a particular town - I cannot remember exactly which one it was - where quite a few Croats were still left. Maybe it was Ilok. That's just an assumption, but I know that quite a few Croats did remain in Ilok, for instance. In that situation, although they were a minority, they were rather restrained and they probably did not want to take part in these activities. I assume that some elections were held there, that it wasn't only appointments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the words of the witness were not accurately translated as to Ilok. He said that many Croats left in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you clarify with the witness, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The -- General, the transcript reads that there were quite a few Croats still left in Ilok. Is that what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said what the gentleman, the attorney, said in his objection. In Ilok, in relation to some other places that I know about, many Croats were left because, from the very beginning, the army played a role there. They wanted to keep the situation as it was. Let me not speak at great length about this now. There were some people from Ilok who left with their weapons, but many returned their weapons and stayed in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And those that stayed in Ilok, what was happening to them in -- in early 1992 that caused problems with regard to them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about specific problems that occurred there. But there were some because on the other side is Backa Palanka, as far as I know. There were attempts made to intimidate some of them so that they'd leave the territory. I know that something happened in relation to the local priest in Ilok. So this was the later stage. Pressure was brought to bear against some of them so that they'd leave the territory. I don't have precise information about this, and I cannot speak about it now, but I am aware of the phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2950, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I just want to look at one more of these Town Command-related documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 6177. It's tab 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a -- an assessment by the 1st Mechanised Corps Command sent to the 1st Military District organ for civilian affairs dated 20 April 1992. And if we take a look at the last page, we see that it's sent by Colonel Novica Gusic. And I would like to draw your attention to page 1 of this assessment, page 2 in the English version. And if we look under item 1, we see much like General Delic, Colonel Gusic is listing a number of problems that they are encountering, and I want to draw your attention, in particular, to item (e) which in the English version is towards the bottom, as well as in the original version. And under (e), Colonel Gusic lists as a problem that: "In the area of Vukovar and Mirkovic municipalities, the SUP has not ensured the protection of personal and social property or full safety of the people through its professional and executive organs for public security. Moreover, it showed no desire to co-operate with this Command in resolving recruitment and the provision of equipment to police units." General, if the local police refused to co-operate with the JNA Town Commands, what recourse did the JNA have?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did what can be seen from the previous two documents. They would report to a higher organ. They were not in charge of resolving the problem by any kind of force. If police -- police stations could not be established, they could not issue a decree or engage in any other activity to appoint the people they wanted to have appointed. They would report to their superiors and that would go all the way up to the command to the Military District, or I don't know -- was already in the army command. I have already explained the army command. Now whether they communicated with the government of the SBWS, then if they could not resolve the problem there, according to General Pujic's instructions, then the army command would resolve that with the government of Serbia, that level. And then by political means this problem would be resolved. So the army was not in charge of establishing any kind of authorities by force. If no result would be achieved, then they would report to their superior command and then that would go all the way up to the government of Serbia, ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know how the -- the local government, the government of SBWS, would respond to these types of problems when they were raised by the military?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Otherwise, in operative terms, I was not involved in these activities because this is not within the purview of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2951, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, under the Vance Plan, who had the responsibility to demobilise and disarm the non-JNA armed elements in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I know what was regulated by the Vance Plan. That is to say, demilitarisation was supposed to take place in the zones where combat activities had been taking place. That is to say, to disband armed units and to have weapons and the equipment of the Territorial Defence placed in storage, double key, the JNA should leave that area. As for these armed units, only the police - milicija - could stay on, and the army was supposed to be on the ready, in a way, if the other side violates the agreement, if there are any incursions coming from the other side. So they would protect the population. Now who was in charge? Everybody was in charge of their own units. The Territorial Defence was supposed to demobilise and disarm their own units. They had the obligation to fully man the new TO units, according to war establishment, or -- we had a meeting. I think it was sometime in April. Maybe we were in Plitvice or somewhere over there, together with the MUP organs and the organs of the Krajina. That is where everything that was needed by this Territorial Defence was taken care of, units, et cetera. The army gave its equipment, weapons, so that they would be fully armed, equipped, but that all this should be in storage in case of an emergency. So everybody had their own obligations. The army was supposed to withdraw and before that to help the local organs establish these units of Territorial Defence and also in materiel terms, to help them. And then the army was supposed to withdraw. And I think that the Territorial Defence also did what they were supposed to do in relation to the units that been armed up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me show you a document. 65 ter 6174. This is tab 199. Sir, this is a 1st Military District document addressed to the Command of the 1st Mechanised, I believe, Corps, and the 12th Corps and it's dated 13 April 1992. And I'd like to draw your attention to item number 1, which states: "With regard to all questions concerning the situation in the territory outside JNA units and their activity, European Community observers should co-ordinate their plans to assess the situation with the government of the Serbian District of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem, but even then they should be accompanied by a liaison officer." General, can you tell us, why is the JNA making this distinction with regard to who is responsible for co-ordinating the plans with the European Commission observers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I see this document, but I can assume that it only acts as a reminder in terms of who was in charge of what. The authorities in the territory have their own responsibility for the work that is supposed to be carried out. I cannot give a more detailed comment because I'm not aware of this, and I did not take part in this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I understand that. But is this consistent with what you understood were the respective roles of the JNA versus the role of the local authority with regard to issues regarding disarmament and demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's clear. I said who was supposed to disarm. They disarmed their own units, that is to say the units of the Territorial Defence that they have. The army reports about how a particular process is evolving in an area where they are so that the command would be kept abreast of what was happening. So there's nothing controversial here. I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because the witness clearly said that he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's consistent with what he was testifying about with regard to obligations under the Vance Plan, with regard to demobilising and demilitarising, with regard to the roles of the JNA versus the role of the local authorities. And he was able to provide some comment on this, and we would tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think this document is not related to disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's an issue for argument, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2952, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, General, and very quickly, I want to return to the issue of crimes in Vukovar after its fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have on the screen, 65 ter 5127. This is tab 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a letter from the British Medical Association to General Kadijevic dated 9 December 1991. The signature at the bottom has been redacted because this document has -- is subject to some protective measures. But let me ask you, the contents deal with persons missing from the Vukovar Hospital after the fall of Vukovar. Could you tell us, in December 1991 or early 1992, were you aware that persons from the Vukovar Hospital were missing after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I know that there were quite a few wounded persons from the Vukovar Hospital at the collection centre in Sremska Mitrovica and that part of the seriously wounded persons were treated at the VMA, the Military Medical Academy and other medical institutions of the military in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As head of the Security Administration, if you were informed of this issue of missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital, what measures would you have taken?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is referred to rather non-specifically. If it says that several persons are missing, then a list should be made as to who these persons who are missing are. This is a rather generalised assessment which is basically incorrect. I think that over 100 wounded persons, persons who were receiving medical treatment, had been evacuated, and I know that they were treated at the VMA and the military hospital in Sarajevo, and in the collection centre itself there were infirmaries where they were treated. This was provided by some, as far as I could interpret this, some group of doctors, some British Medical Association. I see that they are addressing probably General Kadijevic? I don't know who they are addressing. Yes. It is General Kadijevic. I never heard at a single meeting that this question was particularly pointed out and discussed, perhaps because all of these organisations that at the time came to this area and followed the situation, what was going on in Yugoslavia, for the most part, raised problems only from one side, from one angle. We have no information that they indicated such problems in relation to the Serb side. I assume that with regard to these objections, that are rather one-sided in general, they did not even receive an answer. It just says that these persons are missing. In collection centres, there were persons, including persons from the Vukovar Hospital, who were doctors. That just confirms what I've said so far. We did not have any information to the effect that some of the wounded from the hospital had gone missing. They were transferred, some of them to Croatia, some of them to Serbia, or, rather, collection centres there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just clarification in your last answer. You said that some of the wounded persons were treated at the medical centre in Sarajevo. Is that the correct location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Sarajevo. Novi Sad. And the VMA, the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To -- to what end, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I -- I would like to give my explanations, but I think it would be better outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving on to another topic, I don't know if I've understood correctly. Did the witness answer the question which you've just put to him, Mr. Olmsted? Because you asked him whether as chief of security he was informed about the issue of missing persons at the hospital and what measure would you have taken. I don't know if he answered this specific question. I didn't quite understand the witness's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I should ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, General, please, if you could just try to answer it as simply as possible. We understand that you were not aware of this situation where, in this letter, they're reporting about missing persons from Vukovar Hospital. My question to you is simply: Had you been informed of the contents of this letter, that they -- there were a large number of persons missing from the hospital? As head of Security Administration, what actions would you have taken had you had this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not the same question as put before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Nothing wrong with that, Mr. Zivanovic, I would say. If -- if Mr. Olmsted wants to rephrase or focus the question, and Judge Mindua is satisfied with that, what would be the problem? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, I -- you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us simplify. I am not aware of the contents of this document. That would be a simple answer to your question. Had I been acquainted with it, although I don't know along which lines I, as a chief of the Security Administration, should have been, but had I been, I would have demanded this organisation to give me a list of names rather than a general statement that somebody had gone missing. In other words, I would have requested more complete information. And based on what I received from them, I would have taken measures of verification and determination of facts. I don't know if I should reply to anything else because, actually, there were two questions. You asked me what I would have done; and the second question, whether I knew of this. No, I did not know of this. But had I known, I would have requested specific information, who went missing, under which circumstances, and what they know about it. But if what's alluded to - if I may comment - are the persons who went missing at Ovcara, they should have stated that. But obviously at that time they themselves didn't know. They may have heard some accounts but they didn't know. The missing persons for them were Vesna Bosanac and Juraj Njavro and, what do I know, maybe five more doctors. They, as a doctors' association, may have been interested in these people. I suppose that in this text these persons are -- are mentioned somewhere. I haven't read all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, just for the record clear, I just -- just before Mr. Zivanovic objected, I noted that you added a little bit to the content of the letter. I'm reading, page 14, line 13: "My question to you is simply: Had you been informed of the content of this letter that there were a large number of persons missing..." I think the qualification "large" is an addition by yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's an addition by myself but it is self-evident in the letter because it's talking about -- if you do the math it's not like one or two people, it's many more. And maybe I should have qualified it more is what I meant by large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Significant number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This is the letter -- the document we ask you about the reason for tendering and you said you would explain that -- or are we talking about another -- another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's this document, and if -- if -- if I may -- if I can do it outside of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that will be at a later point in time. Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, your time is more than up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I apologise for that, Your Honours, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, my name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I am Goran Hadzic's Defence attorney in these proceedings. I have read your statement, and I listened to your evidence yesterday and today, and I'll ask you some questions about it. I suppose that you have your statement in front of you; 6444 is the number. If you don't have a hard copy, you will see it on the screen. I'll start with item 4 of your statement where you speak about your military career, especially the latter part, that has to do with your work at the Security Administration of the Federal Secretariat of National defence. I saw that from 1986 to 1988, you were head of the counter-intelligence department. Please tell us whose superior you were at the time? I correct myself. Who -- whose subordinate you were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was subordinate to the chief of the Security Administration, General Ilija Ceranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From July 1990, you served as deputy head of the Security Administration. Can you tell me who was head at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major-General Marko Negovanovic was the head of the administration at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that on the 16th of June, 1991, you were appointed head of the Security Administration at the Federal Secretariat of National Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remained in that position until the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, you say that you are proud to have been a JNA officer and proud of any other senior officer who chose this profession of his own free will. Given this attitude of yours towards the JNA, which is not difficult to understand, let me ask you to what extent you can be objective in assessing the activities of the JNA in this context, especially if we talk about some things that give rise to a suspicion that crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be objective to the extent I had information of events, and I can be objective due to the time that has elapsed since, and we're talking about almost 20 years. Now I can look at some events from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, I understand your answer to mean that your attitude towards the JNA does not hinder your ability to analyse the events about which you gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period after the end of my career and after giving evidence, my attitude has not changed significantly. I may have changed my opinion when I learned of some things ten or 15 years after they happened, but when I gave my statement, I gave it on the basis of the information that I had. I don't mean any subsequent corrections. But, in principle, my attitude remains unchanged. This especially pertains to the breaking up of Yugoslavia. In the period from around 1990 until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the General repeat the latter year, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, could you repeat the year you mentioned? From around 1990 until?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, you mentioned some proceedings conducted in Croatia against you. So let me ask you if that fact affects your ability to objectively assess the events?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My opinions when I was in active service and later when I retired, and so on, has remained unchanged. There is no reason for me to change my opinion, and that does not depend on what they allege in their indictment. Why should I change my opinion? I gave their prosecutor replies twice at the War Crimes Court in Belgrade, and I didn't change anything essential before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us be a bit clearer. I did not ask you whether you changed your opinion but to what extent your opinion, your attitude, your way of thinking, or your conclusions about some things, can be objective in the context of these two things I have just mentioned: Your emotional attitude toward the JNA, on the one hand; and the fact that there are proceedings against you in Croatia, on the other.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That didn't influence me at all. Due to these proceedings, I was in the position to review some archive documents. But if you're alluding to the possibility that my statement is affected by the fact that proceedings are conducted against me in Croatia, you can rest assured that this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have some information here that round about 2001 or 2002, a commission was established by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence for co-operation with the ICTY. It was on the 26th of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see D79, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Do you know of the establishment of this commission?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That commission was established - I know that - and it was to provide assistance to witnesses and defendants in proceedings. Let me explain so as not to beat about the bush and waste time. I learned of the indictment against Milosevic when it was published in the media. The persons suspected of participating in a joint criminal enterprise were another four generals, one of whom is me. Although I was a pensioner, I reported to the Security Administration because I do have some duties with regard to the institution I worked for. I reported to be interviewed, but they said that there was no need for that. So -- and I contacted the office of the ICTY of my own accord. They interviewed me, and I informed the general in charge who was a member of that commission of what had happened. I also wrote a report -- actually, I dictated it to a non-commissioned officer who put it on paper. After that, I contacted the Security Administration to inform them because that's where I had served, but they replied that they had already been informed by that commission. And I was angry at that man from the commission to whom I had reported because he was also a security organ at his time. He was even my superior for a while because he didn't tell me he would do so. I encountered resistance. Everybody who wanted to speak out openly about what had happened encountered resistance from -- from within the commission that some things -- that it wasn't necessary to speak out about some things. So that's what I wanted to say. Apart from that, I never set any conditions to ICTY personnel who wanted to talk to me. I never demanded to be taken off the list, and even now I don't know if I've been taken off or not. I gave a witness statement and a statement as a possible suspect, but even if I had been indicted I would have said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that you were indicted together with Milosevic, but --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't say that I had been accused. I'm sure that all four generals had been indicted if I had not volunteered to be interviewed and given a lot of information to clarify the circumstances. And, as far as I know, none of us four were indicted. We were suspects, but so were many others, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this contact with the commission that you've just mentioned, did you have any other contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need. I contacted them and they asked me if I wanted to be a witness, and I accepted. And I told the people from the commission that I would testify. But that required the lifting of my obligation to keep secrets. That was in 2002, and the procedure preceding my evidence drew on, and somebody intervened, I think. Then I was invited to be interviewed by the head of that federal commission, where I explained what I had gone through because I was not informed that I was on the list for interrogation about the events at Ovcara. That was in 1997 or 1998. From the Belgrade War Crimes Court, they asked me if my administration or the General Staff had informed me that I was one of the persons to be questioned about the crimes at Ovcara, but they wouldn't tell me that at the Security Administration. Let me explain. I believe that you are familiar with the situation. In 1992, on the 8th of May, I retired. There was a group of -- a total of 70 generals who retired then. I went to see Milosevic on the 5th of March, 1992, for the first time. I spoke about that at the trial, what the purpose of that meeting was, so I needn't go into that. And I was being shoved aside all the time. Because I'm a frank man I know that people are looking -- people are watching and listening. I have nothing to hide. That's why I acted the way I did, and perhaps I will be convicted if I'm -- if I ever find myself in that situation. So feel free ask me any questions you want that had to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you something else about the work of this commission. Please take a look at another exhibit, D80. It's an analysis of the trial before the Tribunal. It is rather comprehensive. We don't have to go through all of it. But let's take a look at the last page -- actually, the last paragraph of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't mean that. In the English version, this is the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's just the last paragraph where the commission says: "Continue with the preparation of the accused, suspects and potential witnesses before The Hague Tribunal, focussing on the officers in the so-called Operation Dubrovnik ... Operation Vukovar (three persons, Kosovo and Metohija), the officers suspected in connection with the war in Croatia." And among others your name is mentioned too. I would like to know if at least as far as you're concerned what is mentioned here is correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But it is not true that I was informed of it or that anybody proofed me. Because who can proof me? I was head of the Security Administration. I could proof them concerning these things. How can they proof them -- how can they proof me and in what way? So they didn't, nor was I informed of this. I can't see the name because it is blurred but I suppose that General Terzic signed this. He was -- had a lower rank and fewer years of service than I, so he couldn't have known everything that I know. He couldn't prepare me. I don't know if others were prepared. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is something that is striking in the beginning of this paragraph. It says, "Continue with the preparation of," et cetera. One gets the impression that these preparations had already taken place and should just continue. But, all right, you've already answered that question. And you say that you were not being prepared by this commission.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these people - and I was in contact with them - we would see each other even after retirement, at receptions, et cetera, doesn't really matter, in different circumstances. None of them ever told me that they had undergone through these preparations, specifically this Tomislav Simovic. Now why am I saying this? Because Tomislav Simovic responded to the calls of the office of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade and he engaged a Defence attorney for that, and I said, Why do you need a lawyer? I was also in contact with Zivota Panic. I'm not aware of them having undergone any kind of preparations. Perhaps they were given some assistance. Well, I did that too. If I needed some documents that I knew existed then I would address not this commission, I would address the Security Administration so that they could make it possible for me to obtain these documents, and I do not rule out the possibility that they receive these documents or perhaps that they also gave these documents that somebody was involved in that. They knew about Dubrovnik. Somebody would collect everything about Dubrovnik and then they say, Here it is, everything about Dubrovnik. Admiral Jokic is not mentioned here and he was one of the person who was being prepared in the sense of giving him access to documents regarding the Dubrovnik operation. I believe that preparation is not an adequate word, perhaps to be given assistance in their preparations, in my preparations, et cetera. It is in my interest to get the materials I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 of your statement, you said that the eight-member Presidency consisted of a representative from, et cetera, et cetera, and then in 1991 and 1992 you said that you attended three to four meetings between members of the SFRY Presidency and the SSNO. That is paragraph 9 of your statement. You can probably take a look. Now I'd be interested in the following: Was this a meeting of the Presidency or individual members of the Presidency with --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended twice a meeting of the federal council for the protection of the constitutional order that was chaired by Mr. Boro Jovic in the building of the Federal Executive Council with General Kadijevic. So these were meetings where we went, where I went, to these federal institutions. There was a meeting -- as far as I know, there were two meetings. Now if I can remember correctly one was on 4th December, 1991. By then, the Presidency was no longer complete. It was the so-called rump Presidency consisting of Bora Jovic, Bulatovic, Milosevic, and they came to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. There must have been ten other generals present there, but the four of them came to this meeting at the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the rump Presidency," tell me, while you were chief of the Security Administration, that is to say, the 16th of June, 1991, until May 1992, was it always that, as you put it, the rump Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it was complete. Up until the 30th of June. Until the Slovenian situation started. The first problem was that Mr. Stipe Mesic was not elected and verified at the Presidency session. I think that was the 15th of May, 1991. And then the Presidency functioned without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But at that time you were not the chief of security yet.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, I was. The 15th of -- oh. The 15th of May. Fine, yes, I was deputy chief. I know that I came from Zagreb where the investigation was taking place, and he became a member of the Presidency. It was verified at the session that was held on the 30th of June at the insistence of the European Commission that the Presidency had to be completed, and that is why I am saying that the Presidency had to be complete because if it is not complete as the Supreme Commander then it cannot be legal to use the JNA. Who commands the JNA? So on the 30th of June, sometime in the evening he came, and he took over at that session of the council for the protection of the constitutional order. He took over from Boro Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until when this Presidency functioned, including all its members?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already before the Slovenian situation, Mr. Drnovsek did not come to attend meetings. That was the case also on the 12th of March, 1991, when he did not come to this session when the introduction of extraordinary measures and the state of emergency of Yugoslavia were being discussed. He was in fact a member of the Presidency but he did not take part in the work of the Presidency. I cannot remember when this happened exactly. It was after the Slovenian situation. They started distancing themselves because of the war conflict in Slovenia, but I cannot give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Presidency was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces at the time. Now this is what I'm interested in: What happens when there is a rump Presidency, as it is usually referred to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of General Kadijevic was, and we accepted that, was that we always treated the Presidency as the Supreme Commander, regardless of how many member it has. The important thing is that not a single member of the Presidency is prohibited from taking part in its work. Drnovsek does not want to come and attend Presidency sessions but that doesn't mean that Yugoslavia is supposed to fall apart. He had the right to attend sessions of the Presidency and that went for Mr. Mesic and everybody else too. No one was prohibited from doing that. So we respected this other part of the Presidency that continued to function. So this so-called rump Presidency, as people called it, we accepted them as our Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the then-Territorial Defence and the system of command and control in the JNA and the Territorial Defence. You invoked certain articles of the Law on All People's Defence and also of the constitution, so this is what I would be interested in: I have the impression that when you talked about the Law on All People's Defence, you did not take into account its amendments that were carried out in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to this subject matter, although you are not a lawyer, and you don't have to know all these things, but let me see whether you can confirm this. You see Article 110 of this Law on All People's Defence. I think you saw it. It is mentioned here. It is number 13, according to 65 ter. Among other things -- we're probably going to see it on our screen now. Let us just have the English version too, please. Actually, in your statement, you say, in paragraph 11, that the Presidency's orders to the armed forces were passed through the SSNO. That's what your statement says in paragraph 11. I don't know if you have it there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't brought it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If Defence counsel would like, I could provide a copy to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, page 5.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, I think that what it says here is that the Federal Secretariat does not convey orders of the Presidency but commands the armed forces or, rather, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about paragraph 11 from your statement. And now what I have here on the screen is Article 110 of the Law on All People's Defence. And it says here: "The Federal Secretary for National Defence shall exercise the duties of command and control of the armed forces ..." And I think that that is different from what you said, conveys orders, passes on orders.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say passed on or conveyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the last sentence in your paragraph 11, in your statement. In my version, it is page 5.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be of assistance, although I'm not a lawyer. The key thing was that the Presidency of the SFRY was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces; that is to say, of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. If the Presidency of the SFRY as the Supreme Commander transfers the rights of commanding the armed forces, then the Federal Secretariat can command these forces as a whole. If such authority is not given to him, he cannot command these forces. Now this finesse, whether this was transferred, these orders can be transferred by the Presidency. He cannot command on his own so this entire part that we are discussing, there's always this problem, not at a single moment did the function of the Presidency as the Commander-in-Chief stop regardless of whether there were eight of them or four of them. We accepted this Presidency as the Supreme Command. In my statement, later I said that I did not know whether these powers were transferred by the Presidency to the JNA so that the JNA could command the Territorial Defence too. I assumed that that was the case, but I did not have to know about that because at the command post of the 1st Military District we had General Mandaric, who was the provincial secretary, or rather, the provincial commander of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina. According to one article from the Law on All People's Defence, Joint Commands can be established precisely in such situations, that is to say when the right to command the armed forces was transferred to the JNA; then it is good for the command post of the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence Staff should be together with the JNA command. And this position goes through my entire statement and the entire situation as it was. Now whether this right was transferred, I don't know. I assume it was because General Kadijevic probably would not have given orders to the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina too, and put them into the command post of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to torment you with these provisions of the law any longer. I am going to go on to these questions that have to do the general structure of the JNA. You said that in 1987 there was a reorganisation, modernisation of the JNA and that out of the existing five Military Districts, three Military Districts were created, and then there was the naval district and there was the air force and special segments, and these areas of responsibility no longer coincided with the territories of the republics.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say why it was that they no longer coincided with the territories of the republics?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there weren't five Military Districts. There were five armies. And that is a significant difference, whether it's a Military District or an army. If it is armies, for the most part but not completely, they mostly coincided with the republican boundaries. Not exactly, but for the most part. The 5th Army, the Zagreb Army did not have command responsibility over Baranja. From Beli Manastir and Osijek, that was in the area of the Sarajevo Army, the 7th Army, where I was. So this was absolutely not done according to republican borders but for the most part it did coincide. And then the headquarters were in the centres of these areas. In 1987, there was this serious reorganisation of the armed forces that you referred to in terms of the modernisation of the command, adequate placement of units in terms of operative and strategic directions. So in terms of strategic directions -- for example, if there is an aggression from the Warsaw Pact there would not be two armies that would be in that zone of operations. That is one of the reasons why reorganisation took place and why areas of responsibility were made bigger. Then it also had to do with the modernisation of the entire system of defence; that is to say that divisions were abolished as the largest units according to establishment. And the system of corps was introduced, and it consisted of brigades, not divisions. But five independent divisions stayed on as separate units. This caused a problem because just before the crisis that started in the 1990s and continued, some areas were objectively empty. There weren't any units in that area. The most characteristic situation for that was Lika, Kordun, Banja, where, for example, there was a partisan division as an element of a force to be reckoned with. And if you noticed in my statement that I believe it didn't really matter that much to you when officers were sent from the SSNO who started reanimating the units that had been abolished beforehand because this area had been sidelined, if I can put it that way, in terms of consideration from which side threats to Yugoslavia came from. However, some republican leaderships reacted to this situation and their commands were taken, although these commands were never theirs, if I can put it that way. However, in a few armies, army commanders were people precisely from that area and when Military Districts were established, then this was no longer the case. Then the commander of the 5th Military District was a Slovene and the headquarters were in Zagreb. The commander of the 1st Military District was a Croat, and so on. Some republican leaderships and that preceded subsequent to when it started -- reacted and -- and complained that they were being crippled, and so on. That was a mixture of what the army was doing and the -- and the reactions from political circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that in May 1989 - that's in paragraph 30 of your statement - the Presidency of SFRY decided that all assets from TO warehouses are to be transferred to JNA warehouses. Why was this decision taken at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not with the SSNO at that time. I was commander of a division. Now this is -- I'm not saying this by way of defending myself. The Presidency considered that there was a massive misuse with regard to theft of ammunition and weapons. At Prizren, there was a major incident of this kind. Assets from a warehouse were being sold illegally. The former reason was that there was not adequate security and that this must be protected adequately and it was economically and technically best to put all this into JNA warehouses. But, in 1989, in Kosovo, the state of emergency was proclaimed, and that -- those weapons had to be put under control. What I'm talking about was also publicly discussed. And I must say that in all republics of the former Yugoslavia, and not only in Croatia and Slovenia, weapons were placed under the control of the army in army barracks. Only Slovenia did not fulfil this obligation. In 12 municipalities, they did not return these weapons. It was in the region of Gorinsko [phoen]. Now was -- were these weapons taken away from the TO? No. The commander of the TO was able to access those weapons, or even lower levels, such as a captain or so, who had the double keys to the warehouse. But he had to inform the commander of the Military District that they were organising an exercise or a brigade of the TO and that they need weapons. And then it went down the hierarchy and were eventually allowed to take these weapons. In other words, the republican TOs were not left without weapons but the access of those -- to those weapons was regulated. General Novoselic, commander of the Croatian TO, upon the pressure and persuasion of General Spegelj refused to hand over those weapons, although he could have taken the weapons out of the warehouse for exercise purposes, and so on. And, subsequently, I believe that his house which was somewhere near Osijek was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing: When the TO weapons were placed under JNA control, the reorganisation of the army and the reduction of army districts from five to three which triggered negative reactions on the part of some republics, did that forebode an internal conflict in Yugoslavia, which did happen subsequently?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was not assessed not only from that angle but primarily with regard to what was happening in Europe at the time. The Berlin Wall fell. The Warsaw Pact was breaking up. There was unrest in Romania. The president was removed and later killed. All these factors affected our considerations of what was coming. Internally, the multi-party political system was introduced. Various parties emerged, some of which were extremist parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the clock, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, this is the time for our first break. We'll take 30 minutes. Come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will assist you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we have problems with two of the associated documents, and this is about 65 ter 0249 - let's see - which needs -- do I read the number correctly? 02491, sorry. There is translation lacking. So there needs to be some additional translation for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You'll take care of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Absolutely Your Honours, and I'll look at it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And this is another one, and that is 02929 which is unclear. And when we say unclear, we mean unclear in the literal sense. You'll take care of that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'll take care of that as well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, I will continue where I left off with my last question, and I'm sure you can recall it. So my question was this: Did these restructuring measures within the army - not to repeat now the type of measures because you know of that - and the placement of the TO weapons under military control, were they, in a manner of speaking, motivated by the desire to diminish the threat of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now be shown Exhibit 19, please, and this is the document I just mentioned, the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to clarify a couple of things that we can see in these rules. If we can be shown paragraph 6, please. I believe that's on page 6 of the B/C/S version. It says here that security organs are responsible for, and then we see listed a number of activities that they are responsible for. Now, could you tell us what this means exactly, when we say "responsible for"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that they are the chief agents or elements that deal and tackle these issues but they're not the only ones because we also had an evolved system of the so-called social self-protection, and, on the other hand, there were various elements that had certain responsibilities within self-protection that were in the League of Communists, including the chain of command that related to certain elements of the protection of the constitutional order and general security to deal with. Now, if you want me to say what the tasks were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're enumerated here but we don't have to go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are three main tasks, responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you just briefly tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, briefly it is the detection and prevention of intelligence work targeting the armed forces, and so on and so forth. The second portion was the monitoring and detection of activities of enemy activities of the enemy emigration, Yugoslav emigration. That was the second part. And the third was what was then qualified as the activities of the inner enemy, working to subvert the constitutional order. So briefly, in brief, that would be the three basic activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the first group would relate to foreign intelligence services, the second group would deal with emigration - in other words, our people who lived abroad - and the third group dealt with people who were working against the constitutional order but they were active within the country itself. Am I correct? I've sort of simplified this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, you didn't really simplify it. You actually expanded on it. It's not the entire emigration, for instance, but the enemy, the so-called enemy or hostile emigration that was involved in terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this particular portion there is mention, I believe, of the detection of enemy activities by certain individuals and groups. And these individuals and groups would actually relate to those people who would attempt to change the constitutional order in the country by use of armed force.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's the organised portion that deal with that. More often than not, they are organised groups that take action with weapons and arms. And we were involved in detecting these groups from 1991 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Some members of those groups were, later on during the -- during the war, members of the ZNG forces of the Croatian MUP that were later taken prisoner during the war. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. A portion of the extreme emigration after the HDZ won in the elections entered the country legally, although they were still registered as persons who should be detained at the border so that some well-known emigrants from Canada and other parts of the world arrived in Croatia and even assumed some very high positions. There were also those people who were engaged in terrorist activities at their lower level, and they were members, for the most part, of the ZNG. In the first category, I would like to name Gojko Susak, who was in a very important position while President Tudjman was president, and later on during the war I believe he was appointed minister of defence, if I recall that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as part of the work of the security organs, for instance, when dealing with the detained members of the ZNG, their job would be, in fact, to establish the individuals who were, in fact, involved in such activities, that were part of the work of the security organs, as well as those who had committed some crimes, some other crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, among them, there were those who had committed crimes that were both on the -- the jurisdiction of the military security organs and military courts. However, at the time, it was not our priority to establish who the members of the extreme immigration were. Nor the most part we knew the names of those persons and in the final analysis those people actually entered the country legally. So that was not the focus of the work of the security organs. The focus of the security organs's work within these collection centres was to establish, first of all, the identity of all these individuals who were detained because after the first triage and controls, there was an assessment as to who might have been a member of these enemy forces that were involved in activities against the JNA. And in order that to identify that group and those individuals who were there but were not responsible for anything, such individuals were released from the collection centres. As for the other group of individuals, they were then subject to operative processing, and if it was established that they had committed crimes that were not under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary, in other words, that there were minor crimes, such persons would then be exchanged for detained members of the JNA. However, if they were suspected of having committed crimes and serious crimes, those individuals would not be exchanged. Now, the checking of persons, such as in the case of Vesna Bosanac, before she was detained, she was taken and questioned by the investigative judge, and it was then determined that she could be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now move on to the next paragraph. We can see it. We can see the English version of it. But in B/C/S I would ask that we move to the following page. Here it says that security organs participate in and then they list what it is that they participate in, the detection and prevention of serious crimes, and so on and so forth. Could you just distinguish these two things for us? Could you help us understand the difference? In the previous paragraph, it says that the security organs are responsible for, whereas in this paragraph, paragraph 7, it says that security organs participate in certain activities. What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about state security, that's part of the Ministry of the Interior. There's also public security. But, simply speaking, the security organs of the JNA conducted activities from the purview of state security. Other services went about public security, but the security organs were able to participate mostly pursuant to a request of the prosecutor, although somebody else was responsible for that, such as the military police. They could take measures and initiate activities to collect some information that cannot be collected by -- through the activities of public security. Such tasks as detecting such acts follow the -- follow hierarchical lines. They have some powers. But whoever gets information about a crime that has been committed is duty-bound to inform his superior. In the army, you must inform your commander, and then he is duty-bound to take further measures. He can either forward the case to the judiciary or conduct an interrogation from his own purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The activities mentioned in paragraph 7 are done by security organs only when requested to do so, such as by the security organ or the commander or so.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security organs go about operative work. They have their own methods of collecting information from these three areas. If the source of information points out a problem from without the purview of the security organs, and I am -- now I mean the first three, then he is duty-bound to draft a document and inform the commander because the security organs were, in reality, subordinated to the unit commander. And they were duty-bound to -- to provide information even from without their purview when they were in a position to learn of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that your -- that part of your answer was not recorded, but I'll move on to ask you whether that really means that security organs are duty-bound to do the -- this work as described in paragraph 6 without getting special orders or instructions as opposed to the activities in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of these rules of service, we read that the JNA's security organs, as far as the methods of work of these -- these activities, are subordinate to the SSNO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters only have a redacted version of the text. Could counsel please repeat the latter part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you look to the transcript and read the interpreter's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to paragraph 17, the JNA security organs, with respect to the application of methods of -- and tools of work used by these organs, are subordinated to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence or in a -- any senior officer appointed by the secretary. I repeated this part for the record.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat as well. He transferred this authority to some senior officers, not only just before the 1990s, but ever since I have been in service. The security organs are subordinated to the commander -- to the unit commander and not to the superior security organ. That is why. And the right to apply these methods, he transferred to the army commanders and later to commanders of army districts and other senior officers at their level, such as chiefs of General Staff or chiefs of individual sectors at the SSNO, and so on; in other words, the proposal to apply these measures went to the army commander who decided about their use. And he could be briefed about the results of the application of these measures in the same manner as a superior security organ would be, but lower-ranking commanders did not have that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the following section of this same paragraph, the powers of the Federal Secretary in Territorial Defence under the law: "In the Territorial Defence, the commander of the Territorial Defence of a republic or the commander of the Territorial Defence of an autonomous province has the powers of the Federal Secretary under paragraph 1 of this item." In a word, these powers are vested in the commander of the Territorial Defence and this was not transferred to him. This is based on the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the rules of service regulate this aspect. And they had the same powers with regard to heading the security organs as the command -- army commanders in the JNA. The Territorial Defence also had its security organs. These security organs could be transferred from the JNA to the TO, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These officers from paragraph 17 can established provisional groups and send them to garrisons and units to carry out complex intelligence tasks.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were such groups established in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account the -- when this -- these rules of service were published, what they in mind was establishment of KOGs, counter-intelligence groups. And a distinction was made between an operative group which is a military structure and a counter-intelligence group which is a security structure. The later existed -- had their headquarters where they were detached and at that time that you mentioned. There was a counter-intelligence group of the 1st Army in Belgrade, for example, and it had its -- detached security organs in Osijek and other towns. The difference is that these counter-intelligence groups were not subordinated to the commanders in these towns, such as the corps commander or division commander in Novi Sad but they were subordinated to the chief of the KOG in Belgrade. Because they only went about very specific counter-intelligence tasks. And they did not participate in the work of the command. They were in civilian clothes because they weren't part of the commands. And a detachment of a part of the KOG to Sid is in line with this rule, with this provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, a member of a KOG was subordinated to the chief of the KOG.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that chief was really the chief of the KOG at the army district?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinated to the chief of the security -- security department. It's a small unit. It only has ten to 11 people, whereas, a counter-intelligence group headed also by a colonel, could have up to 100 or 110 men or 70 to 80 and they were dispersed to cover the whole territory and deal with security matters. They were numerous. But the head of that counter-intelligence group was professionally subordinated to the chief of the security department of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try and clarify. A member of a KOG, let us say from the 1st Army, or rather, head of one of these departments, to whom was he subordinated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of the KOG of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, chief of the security organ of a unit, such as a corps or brigade, was not subordinated to the chief of the KOG in that territory?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor -- nor did that one need to have contacts with him but could. They are parallel structures. They have different tasks. One provides security to the unit and deals with problems connected with the unit and has three tasks, those three tasks in the territory, whereas the KOG works pursuant to the instructions of the chief of the KOG. If there was a major security problem within a unit, such as an organised enemy group which the operative detected, then the chief of the counter-intelligence department --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters missed part of what you said and they ask you to repeat the last sentence. That means the one you started -- the one just before the one you now started. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. If in a unit there was a major security problem, such as, for example, an organised enemy group, then -- then the operative processing of that group could be done, for example, by a detachment of the KOG from the headquarters, wherever headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now about this last reply. A member of that detachment of a KOG was not subordinated to the chief of security of that unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He is still, in fact, subordinated to the chief of the KOG at the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he sends information to his boss and -- who, in turn, gives him directions, professional directions for his work, although the latter works in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document yesterday, P1865.1. It's a document from the Security Administration dated 26 May 1992. Could we -- or rather, please tell me, I see in the upper left-hand corner -- we see, "Please return after use." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it is the Security Administration that is the source of this information. It is given at the request of the commander and by then it was Zivota Panic, chief of General Staff, so he is the person who ordered the security organs to submit all information to him that have to do with paramilitary units, crimes, and their knowledge about that. They compiled this information, and they submit it to him. All such information is returned to the Security Administration. It could have said up here, Please destroy after use. It could have said that too. However, without a decision of the chief of the General Staff, other persons, his co-workers, could not have been made aware of such information. He could have also given authority to the morale organ to become familiar with that. They are all subordinated to him and carry out tasks issued by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that Zivota Panic was then chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they not subordinated to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, General, the interpreters ask that you should speak a little bit closer to the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this information was provided at the request of General Panic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As chief of General Staff. And they were supposed to be returned once he was made aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, I see that this information was sent when you no longer headed the Security Administration. This information -- or rather, do you know why such information was not requested earlier on while you were at the helm of the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that a problem occurred in relation to the department of the interior because I see that after this, after this information, there was that analysis of what this information says. I assume, I can only assume, that somebody started an initiative. Why was such and such and such not done, and then the chief of General Staff ordered that all of this information be given to the MUP. And then the MUP provided some analysis of their own in response to that. Now, that could have been even some initiative from the military prosecutor's office or from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
