utterances.text: In this information - I think it's already on the next page - there is reference precisely to that crime in Lovas, and -- can we actually move onto the next page, please. First, there is a reference to the Lieutenant-Colonel Dimitrijevic from the Territorial Defence Staff in Valjevo. Do you know whether he was active-duty personnel or whether he was a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, it says that he held the position of co-ordinator for combat activities in the village of Lovas. Can you tell us what that means, "co-ordinator for combat activities"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detachment from the Territorial Defence from Valjevo was resubordinated, sent out into the field, and resubordinated, as far as I know, to the 2nd Mechanised Brigade from the 1st Guards Division. And then from the Territorial Defence Staff, Valjevo, they sent a lieutenant-colonel who would help these reservists, because all of them were reserve officers and reserve soldiers, help them in carrying out their activities. That is, he was supposed to co-ordinate these activities with the 2nd Brigade, too; that is to say he did not have true command responsibility there, to the best of my understanding. Rather, he had the following position. Perhaps I should compare this for the sake of clarity. Like Colonel Pavkovic at the command post of the Guards Brigade, so an officer who was sent from a superior command who was sent to help a particular unit function and resolve problems because he was a more experienced officer. After all, this man was a lieutenant-colonel, and those four officers were all reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is the co-ordinator authorised to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have that kind of authority because objectively they were subordinated to the commander of the 2nd Brigade, and he was the one who could issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because I see here that is says that on the 18th of October at the order of Lieutenant-Colonel Dimitrijevic, and so on and so forth, a group of 50 residents of Croat ethnicity was engaged in sanitising the terrain around the village. I see that this was done in accordances with his order. That's what this document says.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trial at the Belgrade Court has just been concluded with regard to this case. This was done only on the basis of intelligence and only afterwards did an investigation follow and court proceedings, and I don't know what the outcome was. But then there was another trial with all the other members of the Dusan Silni detachment, so I cannot say now that he is the one who issued an order. According to initial intelligence, they were supposed to search the area, and that was supposed to be done by that unit. However, the reservists vacillated and then these volunteers cropped up, and that's how it went. Let me not go into analysis now of the actual situation there. This information was compiled on the basis of some initial intelligence and this intelligence was provided by the Security Administration. As for more complete pictures to what was happening, that could have been requested from the judiciary organs that were involved in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am confining myself to this information that exist until May 1992 because I see this information contained here in this specific document that we have in evidence. I see that according to this information that it had to do with sanitising the area around Lovas, and that 40 members of the TO Valjevo unit detachment took part in this and about ten members of the Dusan Silni detachment under the command of a certain Joca. Since this information was compiled about seven months after the actual event, so during these seven and a half months was any more detailed information received? My impression is that nothing more was learned as compared to what is contained in this information that is written up here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During my previous testimony, I mentioned that this information as mentioned here is not identical to that information number 590 of the 25th of October. Now, when I look at this here in this information, there was no reference to any individual called Joca. Some other names are mentioned, namely persons who were identified by the security organ after the initial interviews. Now, my assessment is that some information was included here that was not only the result of the work of the security organs. Further on in this first information of the 25th October, I don't remember that it was stated that there were 40 of them. So obviously this was some additional information as compared to what was stated on the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the transcript reflects -- perhaps it wasn't transcribed, perhaps it wasn't interpreted, but you said that criminal proceedings were instituted and that some information from these criminal proceedings were included here. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that it is evident from witness statements, eye-witness statements: "That it was known of the existence of the minefield, particularly because it was set up by our units." Also that residents were warned to provide information upon having come across mines and: "Should they try to run away, they would be killed." Did you have information to that effect that these mines were placed there by "our units," as it says here? I mean JNA units by that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This includes information that is not included in that first information of the 25th of October. So I'm convinced even more that this is from the investigation. Minefields were referred to then, but it wasn't stated whether it was the JNA that had laid that there. There was no one else who could have, though, so that was clear, and now this is precisely defined. So this has to do with providing supplement information in relation to the initial information provided that was incomplete, and I am certain that it was from the investigation that was carried out at the time, because there is some information that I had not been aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that it says here - I think it's the third paragraph - that security organs conducted several interviews with Lieutenant-Colonel Dimitrijevic and some other persons. And it says here that the key actors of this event are the members of Dusan Silni and that they left Lovas. I would be interested in the following: When you say that you are convinced that some investigation was being carried out, and that is more than obvious since all these statements were taken, I do not see from here that these persons were identified, the people who left Lovas, these members of Dusan Silni, and I don't see that their names are being provided in this information so that possibly some follow-up action could be taken.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that information of mine dated the 25th of October, the one that I've been referring to, there is a precise reference to names. All eight person, as far as I know. There were eight persons. Now why they are not referred to here, I don't know. But this information did go to the military prosecutor of the JNA, so he knew of those persons as well by name. There weren't any statements then that they had been provided. This was initial intelligence, and that's why I went out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at an R 65, 610 document. It is paragraph 8. I think that it's on the penultimate page, or the last page. Yes, it's the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could Defence counsel provide a tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 610.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But I was asking for a tab, either in your binder or in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that it is in my binder, but I believe it is your binder too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by Zivota Panic, commander of the 1st Military District. I'm interested in paragraph 8. It reads: "Every unit must fully control the situation in the territory of its area of responsibility. Commanders at all levels will be responsible for this. Wartime laws have not entered into force and therefore - as always - nobody has the right to retribution and other kinds of revenge, which some local TO units carried out. In future, arrest these who commit any such acts and undertake appropriate legal measures." You spoke about the jurisdiction of civilian organs, military organs, and others when it comes to crimes. It follows from this order, which was sent to JNA units, that whoever commits crimes in a territory where those military units are must be arrested and that legal measures must be taken against them. This order is dated the 18th of November, 1991. Do you know if the rules and regulation were changed at that time as compared to those that were in force in July or August 19 -- of the same year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that any rules changed, and this would not have been the only order of this kind. There may have been different orders at other levels. Here, some negative occurrences are being pointed out and the situation in the units themselves is not sufficiently known. Before item 8, we see how much ammunition the 46th Partisan Division from Kragujevac had consumed, and it was subordinated to the army; that is, to the 1st Guards Division. It was in the latter zone of responsibility. And I know of some things that happened there. A soldier got killed who changed into civilian clothes, and when he was returning they mistook him for a terrorist. Now it is pointed out here that the situation of units must be known and he reminds the commanders. Let us take a murder which is generally recognised as a crime, and here everybody in the zone of responsibility is responsible in case of such a crime. Now, the local authorities that were in function at the time, that were operational, whether any such letter was sent to them that it was their duty to organise such measures and they had their police stations, and so on, and there was one police station of which Colonel Petkovic had said that he didn't know how they were being set up. However, these people, to whom this is addressed, were not the only ones responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To me, this is a clear order that all those who are guilty must be sanctioned, that measures must be taken against them, which means that there was no legal obstacle for military commanders irrespective of the status of any person as a volunteer or member of a TO, to -- there was no obstacle to launching proceedings against them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the legal provision saying that any person found in the commission of a crime that is prosecuted ex officio must be prosecuted and the judiciary body in charge must be informed. General Zivota Panic didn't go into legal details, although he had good intentions. Of course, the army cannot arrest persons, but they can detain them. And that person, if he is not a JNA member, is transferred to the bodies of the MUP. But there is no problem with this. I don't think that this is the only such order. It's an effort to introduce law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is really why such and similar previous orders were not carried out because we have heard repeatedly that the commander simply failed to act upon such orders.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that previous document we discussed that was sent to General Zivota Panic contains some cases -- some instances of crime, such as rape, plunder, and so on. The perpetrators were not arrested, but the crime sites were secured and the body in charge informed. Talking about the crime at Sotin, I mentioned the person conducting the on-site investigation. Measures were taken, but you couldn't accept the -- you couldn't expect the army to arrest them and keep them and initiate proceedings that were not in its jurisdiction. It was of key importance that the judiciary bodies are informed and then they would decide whom to arrest and whom to transfer to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the following paragraph, number 9, we read that: "All units and formations (volunteers, local communes, et cetera) participating in combat operations in the territory of the 1st Military District must be under the command of the JNA or else they will be disarmed and removed, while extremists will be arrested and appropriate legal measures will be taken." Again, I see that before the order issued by the Presidency, or, more specifically, General Kadijevic, about the disarming of volunteer groups, I see that even before there was such an obligation to place all such groups and units under JNA control. According to your information, why was that not done?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that it wasn't done. That's a general statement. Sometimes it was done, sometimes it was not. At Lovas, it was done, or Sotin, Antin, and other places I have mentioned. This isn't anything new. This is not the first order pointing out this problem. In early December the chief of General Staff issued such an order. All groups and units in this zone of responsibility must be -- either be placed under JNA command or disarmed and removed. And this was issued even before the combat activities on 15 September. And I'm here to say the truth and not speak for the Defence or the Prosecution. Many commanders, in the tactical sense, didn't really cope. Some were unwilling to go into conflict and some engaged in unlawful activity. When there was -- I'll give you an example: In General Blagoje Adzic's order, and that's something generally known anyway, all volunteers had to wear insignia and uniforms of the JNA and respect that aspect, but you saw photographs what the situation was really like. There were guards who were wearing white belts, as if they were military police. So, objectively speaking, there were problems in -- with the line of command because some units in the field did not take strict measures to make sure that this was complied with. General Kadijevic issued an order on the 7th of December, and then on the 10th of December the Presidency took its final decision. But even when these measures were being implemented, I remember that even then all elements of that order were not complied with. What is Arkan doing there? Why is Leva Supoderica still around? In a word, the situation was almost chaotic, and more determination on the part of local commanders was required to impose law and order in respect of their zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, shall we keep your next question for after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. General, 30 minutes again. We will come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could we now take a look at the Law on All People's Defence. That's 3 -- 65 ter number 13. In B/C/S, that would be page 16, whereas in English that's 59. I will only read out paragraph 2 because that's what is relevant here where it says a member of the armed forces is any citizen who is armed or participates in another way in the ... resistance against the enemy. So from this definition, does it follow that all members of the Territorial Defence and volunteer units and similar units that took part in the fighting in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem specifically in 1991, were all these individuals considered members of the armed forces in keeping with this legal provision?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think that this law pertains to a much earlier period which implied -- which only envisaged a situation where the enemy would actually be on the territory of Yugoslavia. That's just a general comment. However, this is only a part of the definition of which individuals are considered to be members of the armed forces. There are other laws such as Article 119, for instance, which deals with volunteers, where it is stated what all conditions have to be met so that a person may be considered a volunteer. It was not a -- it was not sufficient to just bear arms. So there are additional provisions, not just this one, and they were contained both in the orders which came from the General Staff but also the Presidency which dealt with who was to be considered a volunteer and -- let alone a member of the armed forces. To -- to simplify this, not to be banal, but to simplify it, you couldn't just carry hunting weapons and be considered a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are not a lawyer so I will not enter into a debate with you on this, but, according to this formulation, a person is to be considered a member of the armed forces if they take part in the resistance against the enemy not necessarily carrying arms. So this would pertain to any citizen, whether volunteers or not, if I read this correctly. Could you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as layperson I do not want to enter in a polemic. But this would mean that -- well, any armed person in a combat area would have to be subordinated to a military command in order to be considered a member of the armed forces, but let's not polemicize on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, in the second paragraph of 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army considered the Croatian armed forces as an enemy force; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA considered those forces, forces that had engaged in an armed rebellion. Now, objectively and factually they were the enemy because there was armed combat with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the volunteers who were, for instance, in the Operations Group South area of responsibility that they were placed under the command of that operations group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that in the order of -- for engagement of the south operations group and the Leva Supoderica detachment was part of the detachment 1, the Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit 779, or, actually, 65 ter 779, page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the third paragraph. Let me just check something. That's the penultimate paragraph in the English version. It says there that: "In addition to the Guards Motorised Brigade the Vukovar and Leva Supoderica detachments a large number of volunteers participated in the fighting." The work and sending of volunteers in the -- in the zone was not organised. They arrived in group -- volunteers arrived in groups and in a disorganised manner: "Our unit had major problems with receiving them, checking and equipping them, and employing them in combat. A large number of volunteer arrived with party insignia, which might have had considerable effects on the order and discipline of the units conducting combat tasks. Through daily and relevant activity, we succeeded in placing all the volunteers under JNA command, or rather, under the OG South Command." What is the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecutor showed this to you when he showed your report. Perhaps we can see the first page. I believe this is a report submitted by Major Sljivancanin on the 10th of December, 1991. I will show you another report by the same individual. You were shown that report yesterday by the Prosecutor as well. And that is 65 ter 483 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check the English version. It appears that the translation into English is not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out the entire text to you, and then you can see this. It says here: "On the 23rd of October, 1991, because of what blatant cowardice and mass opportunism, 70 volunteers were disarmed and dismissed and the dismissal of another 60 volunteers has been announced." This is a report submitted by the security chief from the office of the Federal Secretary of National Defence reporting on the situation with security within the units, an area of responsibility of the Guards Motorised Brigade. And I see that this practice of disarming of volunteers was already evident in October, but I also see that one of the reasons for that was cowardice and mass opportunism. Now, I don't know exactly what this was supposed to mean, but let me put my question, then you'll understand why I show this to you. It would seem that volunteers were disarmed and dismissed easily if they did not participate in combat as they should and that the dismissal was far less frequent if they were -- if their conduct was contrary to some laws and rules.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can I perhaps answer? Volunteers arrived from various parts and in various ways. You probably know from the documents available that there were reception centres for volunteers that were established in the beginning. There were two such centres. There, they were trained briefly, and then they were sent in an organised manner to various units. Now, what we are talking about here are two kinds of volunteers, and Major Sljivancanin is talking about one of them. He is discussing volunteer who came and joined the Guards Brigade unit from various parts and in various manners and is he not referring to volunteers that established their own units and had their own unit names. He is talking about the dismissal of volunteers from the brigade itself without going into the details of what the volunteers' situation was like within units like Leva Supoderica, and so on, or volunteers who had come through the TO Staffs. These were volunteers that were assigned to the brigade from various parts and in various manners. Now, when I went to Dalj to be briefed, we were also shown information about losses. But in daily reports of the OG South, you can see that there is also discussion of losses, where they would point out how many officers and JNA soldiers were killed or wounded and then there would be mention of volunteers and then below that, it would say "Chetniks." In other words, those who arrived without any insignia, who came to = the brigade but were not part of it. They engaged in action together with the brigade but not as part of it. So there was this division and this distinction of volunteers when I was in Dalj, so please be aware of this. Those who joined the brigade as volunteers they became JNA soldiers. There were some of them who were not brave who realised that people died there and also all such individuals who displayed cowardice or who were unsure and uncertain, they were dismissed. But these were not dismissals of volunteer who arrived there as member of some other unit; for instance, the Leva Supoderica or any other unit was subordinated to the JNA during fighting but once the fighting was over, they were no longer under the -- under the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's something that we will clarify in a moment. In any case, I don't see a major difference between those volunteer who came in one way or another, who were members of one unit or another. They were within the same complement and the commanders had the same authority over them so they could disarm or dismiss either ones. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They did not have the authority to disarm a group who came from who knows where, from some part of Vukovar or some other place, like Lovas, for instance. Let's go back to Lovas. There is the Ljuban Devetak group in Lovas that was not part of the JNA, and they did not disarm that group as such because that's the kind of group it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies for interfering, but we're talking about the Guards Motorised Brigade. So let's not go to Lovas or any other area there. Let's just focus on the brigade. So the commander of this brigade was authorised -- had the authority over all the volunteers who were there. Irrespective of the manner that they arrived there, he had authority to disarm or dismiss them or to punish them, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he could not punish them. There was no grounds for punishing them. If they refused to fight, what would be the grounds for his punishing them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, but if they commit crimes or infractions, then they could punish them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, he could punish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading this material, I see that you said yesterday - and that's on page 7955 of yesterday's transcript - that volunteers were called up because the JNA could not replenish its units. It could not man its units properly. And it is my impression on reading this that those who fought were tolerated even if they committed some criminal act and only those who were incapable of fighting, they were the ones who were returned. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. Because -- well, you also said that these people would be tolerated even if they created problems. I wouldn't agree with that. The problem we're talking about - in other words, who was subordinated to whom - that's where the issue is. In Vukovar, on the 21st, the combat ended. The volunteers then broke into JNA barracks because of the buses that had arrived there with the prisoners from the hospital, and they created chaos there. Colonel Panic at the time who was the chief of the barracks arrived there then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to stop you here. You weren't there at the time, on the 21st of November, as you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard about this later on from various sources.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while reading the transcript of the proceedings here. So I'm an indirect witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I'm trying to put to you, and I don't have too much time, is this: There is no need for you to refer to these transcripts because we've read most of them and we're familiar with them, both in this case and in some earlier cases. But could you just clarify something to us? The subordination, the chain of command within combat operations or during combat operations, what did that mean practically; for instance, during the Vukovar operation? From what point in time were these territorial units and volunteers under the command, or rather, subordinated to OG -- to the OG. Or perhaps even clearer or more pointedly, up until when would they be subordinated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as long as the combat was ongoing they would be subordinated. The combat is carried out upon an order, and everyone is assigned a task. Once a task is completed, they should return to their original unit. In other words, this unit would no longer be responsible for them, because this is outside of the combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, when did combat activities end in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar on the 19th of November, in the evening. I had contact with Sljivancanin and the security organs. They told me that the combat was over. So, according to that, it would have been the 19th or a previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they give any orders to that effect to the Vukovar TO or Leva Supoderica, saying that their task was accomplished? You said that they would either return to the original unit or be resubordinated to another JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed that with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I'm going to show you a document. It's 1995. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 1995.1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued on the 21st of November, 1991, at 6.00 a.m. It is about the resubordination and the return to the original units. And it says under item 1 that: "In the course of the 21 November 1991, withdraw the Leva Supoderica volunteers detachment and dispatch them, resubordinate them, to the 12th pmbr." Does that mean that until that time this detachment was subordinated to OG South?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at item 4: "Vukovar TO units to be resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade and continue with carrying out the assigned tasks - the provision of security and the control of the captured areas in Vukovar, with an emphasis on the most sensitive facilities (municipality, post office, SUP, educational and cultural facilities)." Does that mean that at that time TO -- Vukovar TO units were resubordinated to OG South?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't say that the unit in question was part of OG South. It only says where it is supposed to go. I suppose that, since it was there all the time, it was with OG South, but -- I see you're smiling so I'll follow your example. I saw some documents about -- saying what was going on. Nobody ever reported where they were supposed to report. They stayed behind and did what they pleased. Then approval was given to the command of the 1st Army to disarm the Leva Supoderica, and this is very telling as to how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you please take a look at paragraph 4. This is what it says there. The TO Vukovar units should be resubordinated to the 80th Brigade and continue with carrying out the assigned tasks. Does that mean that until then they had some tasks and on that 21st of November at 6.00 in the morning, these tasks were still under way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see what it says here? Provide security for the municipality, post office, water works, et cetera. These are typical tasks for a TO unit, very correctly defined. Again I have to say, what is this unit doing on the 21st? Where is it? Is it providing security for buildings or is a considerable part of this unit at Velepromet and at the barracks when the buss arrived. All of this is regulated and written just fine but we are talking about the actual state of affairs. I am defending one thing: What happened. What actually happened. And then you have what it was regulated like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, on the 21st of November, I really don't know where this unit was deployed but I know where its commander was. Do you know whose commander it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The TO Vukovar unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they changed at least once. I may be making a mistake when I say Dusan Jaksic, perhaps that was not the case, or how should I know? Was it that Ljubinko? What was it, Stojanovic? I don't know who the commander is. I cannot say with certainty now because they changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have some information to the effect that on the 21st of November, General Kadijevic, received a group of officers from the 1st Military District, or rather, from the Guards Brigade, and among these persons was also the commander of the TO of Vukovar. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the reception. I was shown some footage from that reception here. There was a man from Territorial Defence there. I cannot confirm his first or last names, and it's not that I could recognise him. I think that he had a bandage on his hand or arm. He was wounded but it wasn't in combat but in some kind of fight, so this reception did not last for very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, this order that we looked at just now, do you consider it to be the order that is supposed to follow after combat, either in order to have that unit returned to its original units, or for it to be resubordinated to another JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I think because the same kind of order had to be there when they were resubordinated to Operation Group South. And also when it is no longer necessary to engage them, then this kind of order is made because someone cannot leave without knowing on what grounds. So I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now take a look at the bottom of this page, this order. It says that it was made in eight copies and that it was submitted to, first of all, the commander of the volunteer unit, Seseljevci, Seselj's men. Who is this commander of the volunteer detachment "Seseljevci?" Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no dilemma in my mind that this is the Leva Supoderica detachment. Because at these levels, different expressions were used. Even the chief of General Staff in an order speaks about armed units of the Republic of Croatia and then in relation to that same document, the political administration says, armed Ustashas. So they used the word "Ustashas," and the chief of General Staff says "the armed forces of the Croatia." Or here, often Leva Supoderica is referred to, that detachment, and they call them Seseljevci, Seselj's Men. So I have no doubt in my mind that this has to do with that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that yesterday you spoke about your notebook and your contact with General Babic in Sid, or was it Petkovic - I'm sorry, I may have forgotten a bit - in Sid. And you say that you recorded that meeting in your notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at that. It's 495. That is the exhibit number from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2917.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that this is a pass issued to comrade, as it says, Djordje Neznanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try and clarify this because the terminology probably isn't clear. This word "comrade" was used in the former SFRY instead of mister, which is used now. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At some point, comrades became gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a bit unusual for people from a Chetnik unit to be termed that, a Chetnik unit such as Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual way to address persons was comrade. This isn't special in any way, has nothing to do with the status of the unit. The fact that they were members of the Serbian Radical Party doesn't mean that they are no longer comrades. It was the jargon of the time. I don't think it has any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they use that jargon themselves?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if Mr. Seselj was Comrade Seselj from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard anyone from his party addressing him as Comrade Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never paid attention to the way they communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you didn't have any specific knowledge about the certificate but you offered us your understanding of it. Let me ask you if it is your impression that this certificate, or rather, pass, as it says, is in line with the order issued by Colonel Mrksic under which Leva Supoderica is resubordinated to the 12th Corps. Do you see any coincidence there in terms of dates?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is different, and I was going to comment on that. In the morning, at 6.00, he got an order to resubordinate to the 12th Brigade, which means that as soon as the 22nd he was supposed to be at Dalj, or wherever that brigade was. But on this day indicated here, he is giving leave to this person who is supposed to return his weapons. But this fact has nothing to do with the -- this location. The entire unit, as it was, had to be resubordinated. So there is no connection here. I can only tell that on the 22nd he was still there rather than at the 12th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell that he is there. Are you referring to Lancuzanin?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His deputy, which means the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And where, there, at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because this is the stamp of the Guards Brigade which was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can this mean that this man decided to leave Leva Supoderica and go home?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this is exactly the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This time when he's returning what was issued to him, does it coincide with the time when the Guards Brigade was leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Guards Brigade withdrew a few days later, on the 24th, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did such persons, as the one whose name we read here and who had the same status, did they get any sort of compensation or benefits from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they should be -- should have received some. The last time I went to Vukovar, I went there due to problems created by some armed members, probably members of Lancuzanin's units, judging by the insignia they wore and the kokardes. They didn't want to return what was issued to them because they -- they didn't get any money on that occasion. The purpose of this certificate was that the person mentioned in there was a legitimate member of the armed forces and that they got some financial compensation. This is a certificate enabling the person in question to leave the combat zone because there was still check-points. And the certificates for the purpose of proving participation in war were like the ones we saw for those two from Lovas, showing that they were -- that they were there until January or February. They also enjoyed some benefits and some -- some rights that they still have today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that the JNA disbursed some money to this very person roughly at the time when he returned what was issued to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to the 1D553 but it should not be shown to the witness and the public. It is paragraph 29, page 7. Sorry, I said it should not be shown to the witness and to the public. It is on our exhibit -- on our list for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see the first page just briefly. And we can move to the page -- to paragraph 29. It's page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot reveal the source of information because our rules prohibit that. But, according to that information, before leaving Vukovar - that is, before the 22nd of November - this person got some money from the JNA. Only then did he return his weapons and equipment and then left. Is that in line with your information about the way that money was paid to members of this detachment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment this specific example on this unit. I know the general rule, and it was honoured. Those who took part in combat as members of a JNA unit were paid out compensation. To receive it, they needed to provide a certificate from the unit, and their military booklet also needed to have an entry that from, till, they were members of military post number so-and-so. If he had a military booklet, then I'm sure that this information was entered there. Then lists of such persons were made, and they got what was due to them. There's no problem with that, to my mind. He was a member of Leva Supoderica, which, under the Command of OG South, took part in combat, and he had the same rights of any soldiers of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now return to the report dated 10 December 1991. You know which report I mean, the one Major Sljivancanin sent to you on 10 December.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that in that report he mentions that the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem appointed TO commanders who were not respected by the people and who engaged in dirty business. And I believe that you answered the Prosecutor's question that this was in line with the information that you had. Tell me, did that information originate from this report by Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there was a time when I didn't have that information but on the basis of documents about the establishment of Town Commands, some people were complaining - and I think that this was from the 1st Guards Division - that people were being appointed who lacked the qualities required for those positions. And then there was resistance on the part of the population, and so on. There was such information, so Sljivancanin's report was not the only source, nor was it all from the period you're referring to. There was information that there were criminal-minded people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would limit myself to the Guards Brigade and his reports, so I would -- don't want to go into other reports for the time being. Did you ever find out - and I'm referring to that period in that area - which TO commanders were appointed by the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any appointments made by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago -- or, rather, we were talking about the commander of the TO Vukovar, Jaksic, and you said what reasons were provided for asking for his dismissal. But you were not told that he was involved in some kind of crime. My understanding was that you were told that he was too passive.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they reacted on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it is not crime that was the reason for his dismissal.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I was told then or what was explained to me then. It was only the things that I have stated just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would change the topic, and I see the clock, and maybe we could make the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. General, we finish for the day. You -- we expect you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, as Mr. Zivanovic has not finished yet, and there are eventually questions in re-direct and questions from the Judges. You are -- you remain under oath, which means, as I explained to you yesterday, that you cannot discuss your testimony to -- with anybody, and you cannot talk to any of the parties. Thank you very much. The Court Usher will escort you out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.
